messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 39

He is a 24-year-old Southeast Asian man who comes across as careful and soft-spoken, with a habit of watching the door and checking a room before settling into it. He works as a painter, and he talks about color and texture with more ease than he talks about himself. Before the relationship that changed him, he describes being energetic, affectionate, and proud of how steadily he was building a life with his partner. He remembers feeling lucky to be loved so intensely at first. The attention felt flattering, even protective, and he mistook control for devotion.

The abuse begins gradually. At first it is criticism, then humiliation, then grabbing his wrist too hard, shoving him into a wall, slapping him when he says the wrong thing or asks to leave an argument. He learns to read the other person’s moods the way he reads the light in a room before starting a painting. He begins choosing words carefully, shortening his answers, staying quiet. He tells himself that if he is more patient, more understanding, the volatility will pass. Instead, it escalates. He starts losing track of time during arguments because his mind goes blank, and afterward he feels ashamed of how still he becomes. He says he often felt as if he were “watching from far away” while it was happening, which helped him survive in the moment but left him feeling unreal afterward.

After one especially violent episode, he leaves with a split lip and soreness in his ribs, telling coworkers he slipped. He does not want anyone to know. He keeps working because painting is the one place he feels competent and hidden at once. He can climb ladders, mix colors, and cover a wall in even strokes without having to explain himself. But after the assault, even ordinary parts of the job begin to feel changed. He startles when someone comes up behind him unexpectedly. The sound of a door slamming in a client’s home makes his stomach drop. He finds himself tense around tools that could be thrown or used as weapons, though no one at work is threatening him. At times he notices that his hands shake when he is trying to cut a clean line, and he has to stop and breathe until it passes.

He leaves the relationship in pieces rather than all at once, which he describes with both relief and guilt. He misses the person he thought he was with before the violence became constant, and he also misses the version of himself who did not flinch at a raised voice. Even after the breakup, he keeps expecting contact, punishment, or apology. When his phone buzzes, his body reacts before his mind does. He reads messages over and over, trying to figure out whether he is being manipulated again. He avoids places that remind him of the worst fights, especially certain streets, music, and the apartment where he used to sleep with his shoes on near the bed. He says there are days he drives a longer route home just to avoid passing that building.

In the months after leaving, sleep becomes difficult. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes on alert, sometimes from dreams he cannot fully remember but that leave him sweating and disoriented. He braces himself in the dark, listening for footsteps, and his mind returns to details he wishes he could erase: the feel of a hand on his throat, the sound of himself apologizing to make it stop, the look on the other person’s face just before the blow. During the day, he is often flooded by images that arrive without warning. A smell of paint thinner, a certain cologne, or a sudden sharp sound can pull him back into the fear so completely that he has to sit down and wait for the wave to pass. He does not talk about these moments easily, but when he does, he speaks as though the events still belong to the present.

He is now in another relationship, and he cares deeply about his partner, but trust does not come naturally. He checks for signs of anger, interprets silence as danger, and apologizes quickly even when he has done nothing wrong. He wants closeness and fears it at the same time. He says he is trying to learn how to let his body understand what his mind already knows: that not every raised hand is meant to hurt, and not every argument ends in violence. For now, he moves through his days with a guarded steadiness, working, loving, and measuring safety in small, hard-won moments.
